claim: GIRK channels control spike frequency in atrial pacemaker cells.
source: GIRK channels control spike frequency in atrial pacemaker cells and inhibitory potentials in neurons.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about GIRK channel function in cardiac cells.

claim: GIRK channels control inhibitory potentials in neurons.
source: GIRK channels control spike frequency in atrial pacemaker cells and inhibitory potentials in neurons.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about GIRK channel function in neurons.

claim: GIRK directly responds to G proteins.
source: By directly responding to G proteins, PIP2 and Na+, GIRK is under the control of multiple signaling pathways.
evidence: This statement in the abstract is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript showing direct effects of G proteins on GIRK2.

claim: GIRK directly responds to PIP2.
source: By directly responding to G proteins, PIP2 and Na+, GIRK is under the control of multiple signaling pathways.
evidence: This statement in the abstract is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript showing direct effects of PIP2 on GIRK2.

claim: GIRK directly responds to Na+.
source: By directly responding to G proteins, PIP2 and Na+, GIRK is under the control of multiple signaling pathways.
evidence: This statement in the abstract is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript showing direct effects of Na+ on GIRK2.

claim: Mammalian GIRK2 channel has been purified and reconstituted in planar lipid membranes.
source: In this study, the mammalian GIRK2 channel has been purified and reconstituted in planar lipid membranes and effects of Gα, Gβγ, PIP2 and Na+ analyzed.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental approach used in the study, supported by the methods section.

claim: Gβγ and PIP2 must be present simultaneously to activate GIRK2.
source: Gβγ and PIP2 must be present simultaneously to activate GIRK2.
evidence: This conclusion is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Na+ is not essential for GIRK2 activation but modulates the effect of Gβγ and PIP2 over physiological concentrations.
source: Na+ is not essential but modulates the effect of Gβγ and PIP2 over physiological concentrations.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Gαi1(GTPγS) has no effect on GIRK2 channel activity.
source: Gαi1(GTPγS) has no effect, whereas Gαi1(GDP) closes the channel through removal of Gβγ.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Gαi1(GDP) closes the GIRK2 channel through removal of Gβγ.
source: Gαi1(GTPγS) has no effect, whereas Gαi1(GDP) closes the channel through removal of Gβγ.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: In the presence of Gβγ, GIRK2 opens as a function of PIP2 mole fraction with Hill coefficient 2.5.
source: In the presence of Gβγ, GIRK2 opens as a function of PIP2 mole fraction with Hill coefficient 2.5 and an affinity that poises GIRK2 to respond to natural variations of PIP2 concentration.
evidence: This quantitative result is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: GIRK2 has an affinity for PIP2 that poises it to respond to natural variations of PIP2 concentration.
source: In the presence of Gβγ, GIRK2 opens as a function of PIP2 mole fraction with Hill coefficient 2.5 and an affinity that poises GIRK2 to respond to natural variations of PIP2 concentration.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing the apparent dissociation constant is ~0.8% mole fraction.

claim: The dual requirement for Gβγ and PIP2 can help to explain why GIRK2 is activated by Gi/o, but not Gq coupled GPCRs.
source: The dual requirement for Gβγ and PIP2 can help to explain why GIRK2 is activated by Gi/o, but not Gq coupled GPCRs.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation stated in the abstract and discussed in detail in the Discussion section, drawing on the experimental findings and prior knowledge.

claim: GIRK channels are inward rectifier K+ (Kir) channels whose activity is regulated by GTP binding proteins (G proteins).
source: G protein gated inward rectifier K+ (GIRK) channels are inward rectifier K+ (Kir) channels whose activity is regulated by GTP binding proteins (G proteins) (Brown and Birnbaumer, 1988; Yamada et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: GIRK channels are present in many different cell types including electrically excitable cells in the cardiovascular and nervous systems.
source: They are present in many different cell types including electrically excitable cells in the cardiovascular and nervous systems (Dascal et al., 1993; Lesage et al., 1994; Krapivinsky et al., 1995; Lesage et al., 1995; Karschin et al., 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: GIRK channels regulate cellular electrical activity by modulating K+ conductance near the resting membrane potential.
source: GIRK channels regulate cellular electrical activity by modulating K+ conductance near the resting membrane potential.
evidence: This is a functional description based on established knowledge of GIRK channel biophysics.

claim: Stimulation of certain G protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) on a cell's surface leads to the opening of GIRK channels, which increases K+ conductance and opposes the initiation of action potentials.
source: Specifically, stimulation of certain G protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) on a cell's surface leads to the opening of GIRK channels, which increases K+ conductance and opposes the initiation of action potentials.
evidence: This is a mechanistic description based on established knowledge of GIRK channel function.

claim: Vagus nerve stimulation slows heart rate through acetylcholine action on GPCRs in atrial pacemaker cells.
source: This inhibitory effect on excitation is best understood in the cardiovascular system, where vagus nerve stimulation slows heart rate through acetylcholine action on GPCRs in atrial pacemaker cells (Loewi and Navratil, 1926; Giles and Noble, 1976; Osterrieder et al., 1981).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to classic studies in cardiac physiology.

claim: Activation of GIRK channels prolongs the interval between pacemaker action potentials, thus causing the heart rate to slow.
source: The ensuing activation of GIRK channels prolongs the interval between pacemaker action potentials, thus causing the heart rate to slow.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on established knowledge of cardiac pacemaker physiology.

claim: GIRK channels are abundant in the nervous system.
source: GIRK channels are also abundant in the nervous system, where they modulate slow inhibitory postsynaptic currents in response to neurotransmitter stimulation (Luscher et al., 1997; Lujan et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: GIRK channels modulate slow inhibitory postsynaptic currents in response to neurotransmitter stimulation.
source: GIRK channels are also abundant in the nervous system, where they modulate slow inhibitory postsynaptic currents in response to neurotransmitter stimulation (Luscher et al., 1997; Lujan et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The G protein 'subunit' called Gβγ (a tightly bound complex of β and γ protein polypeptides) is the major mediator through which GPCR stimulation opens GIRK channels.
source: First, the G protein 'subunit' called Gβγ (a tightly bound complex of β and γ protein polypeptides) is the major mediator through which GPCR stimulation opens GIRK channels (Pfaffinger et al., 1985; Logothetis et al., 1987; Reuveny et al., 1994; Wickman et al., 1994; Huang et al., 1995; Inanobe et al., 1995; Kofuji et al., 1995; Krapivinsky et al., 1995).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature establishing Gβγ as the key mediator.

claim: When a GPCR is stimulated through the binding of a neurotransmitter (or drug) on the outside of the cell membrane it catalyzes guanine nucleotide exchange–GTP replaces GDP on the Gα subunit–and release of Gα(GTP) and Gβγ subunits on the cytoplasmic side.
source: When a GPCR is stimulated through the binding of a neurotransmitter (or drug) on the outside of the cell membrane it catalyzes guanine nucleotide exchange–GTP replaces GDP on the Gα subunit–and release of Gα(GTP) and Gβγ subunits on the cytoplasmic side (Gilman, 1987).
evidence: This is a description of the canonical G protein activation cycle, supported by citation to foundational work.

claim: Gβγ activates GIRK.
source: These subunits are then free to activate their 'target' proteins: Gβγ activates GIRK.
evidence: This statement is supported by the experimental data in this study and prior knowledge.

claim: The signaling lipid phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) also regulates GIRK channel opening.
source: Second, the signaling lipid phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) also regulates GIRK channel opening (Huang et al., 1998; Sui et al., 1998; Logothetis and Zhang, 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: GIRK channels respond to more than one ligand and thus are under the control of more than one distinct signaling pathway.
source: This property means that GIRK channels respond to more than one ligand and thus are under the control of more than one distinct signaling pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the multi-ligand regulation of GIRK channels.

claim: The activity of certain GIRK channels, for example the neuronal GIRK2 channel, is also regulated by the concentration of intracellular Na+.
source: Third, the activity of certain GIRK channels, for example the neuronal GIRK2 channel, is also regulated by the concentration of intracellular Na+ (Petit-Jacques et al., 1999; Ho and Murrell-Lagnado, 1999a, 1999b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Intracellular Na+ concentration increases during excessive electrical excitation.
source: Intracellular Na+ concentration increases during excessive electrical excitation.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge of cellular physiology.

claim: Activation of GIRK2 under conditions of increased intracellular Na+ may serve as a cell protective mechanism through action potential suppression.
source: Activation of GIRK2 under this circumstance may serve as a cell protective mechanism through action potential suppression.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of Na+ regulation.

claim: X-ray crystallography has recently provided atomic level descriptions of a neuronal GIRK channel, GIRK2, in the absence and presence of Gβγ, PIP2 and Na+.
source: Finally, x-ray crystallography has recently provided atomic level descriptions of a neuronal GIRK channel, GIRK2, in the absence and presence of Gβγ, PIP2 and Na+ (Whorton and MacKinnon, 2011, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: The Gα subunit co-precipitates with GIRK in biochemical 'pull-down' experiments.
source: The Gα subunit co-precipitates with GIRK in biochemical 'pull-down' experiments (Huang et al., 1995; Peleg et al., 2002; Ivanina et al., 2004; Rubinstein et al., 2009; Berlin et al., 2010, 2011) and also exhibits interaction with the channel's cytoplasmic domain as detected by solution NMR spectroscopy (Mase et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior biochemical studies.

claim: Gα exhibits interaction with the GIRK channel's cytoplasmic domain as detected by solution NMR spectroscopy.
source: The Gα subunit co-precipitates with GIRK in biochemical 'pull-down' experiments (Huang et al., 1995; Peleg et al., 2002; Ivanina et al., 2004; Rubinstein et al., 2009; Berlin et al., 2010, 2011) and also exhibits interaction with the channel's cytoplasmic domain as detected by solution NMR spectroscopy (Mase et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to a prior NMR study.

claim: PIP2 is a signaling lipid whose concentration in the cell membrane changes.
source: PIP2 is a signaling lipid whose concentration in the cell membrane changes (Lemmon, 2008; Balla, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature on PIP2 dynamics.

claim: There are four binding sites for PIP2 on each GIRK2 homotetramer.
source: There are four binding sites for each of these ligands on each GIRK2 homotetramer.
evidence: This statement is made in the Figure 1 legend and is based on the crystal structure shown in the figure.

claim: There are four binding sites for Na+ on each GIRK2 homotetramer.
source: There are four binding sites for each of these ligands on each GIRK2 homotetramer.
evidence: This statement is made in the Figure 1 legend and is based on the crystal structure shown in the figure.

claim: There are four binding sites for Gβγ on each GIRK2 homotetramer.
source: There are four binding sites for each of these ligands on each GIRK2 homotetramer.
evidence: This statement is made in the Figure 1 legend and is based on the crystal structure shown in the figure.

claim: Brief channel openings appear as downward current spikes because the membrane voltage was held positive relative to ground and the sign of current was inverted to conform to electrophysiological convention.
source: Brief channel openings appear as downward current spikes because the membrane voltage was held positive relative to ground (top chamber, Figure 1B) and the sign of current was inverted to conform to eletrophysiological convention.
evidence: This is an explanation of the experimental recording convention used in the study.

claim: When PIP2 was added to GIRK2 channels in the absence of Gβγ, channel activity remained essentially unchanged.
source: When PIP2 was added to the top chamber half way through the trace, channel activity remained essentially unchanged (Figure 2B).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Addition of Gβγ in the absence of PIP2 did not perceptibly alter baseline GIRK2 channel activity.
source: Similarly, addition of Gβγ in the absence of PIP2 did not perceptibly alter baseline channel activity (Figure 2C).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Only when both PIP2 and Gβγ were present, independent of the order in which they were added, did large K+ currents due to robust GIRK2 channel opening occur.
source: Only when both PIP2 and Gβγ were present, independent of the order in which they were added, did we observe large K+ currents due to robust GIRK2 channel opening (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2D and 2E.

claim: In the bilayer assay, PIP2 or Gβγ alone are insufficient to elicit robust GIRK2 channel activation.
source: It is thus clear in the bilayer assay that PIP2 or Gβγ alone are insufficient to elicit robust channel activation.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the experimental observations in Figure 2.

claim: Both PIP2 and Gβγ ligands together are necessary to open GIRK2 channels.
source: Both of these ligands together are necessary.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the experimental observations in Figure 2.

claim: Past studies had reached the conclusion that both PIP2 and Gβγ ligands are important—that one ligand enhances the affinity of the other.
source: While past studies had reached the conclusion that both ligands are important—that one ligand enhances the affinity of the other (Huang et al., 1998; Yamada et al., 1998; Logothetis and Zhang, 1999)—the complexity of cell membranes obscured the simple conclusion so obvious here that both ligands are necessary to open the channel.
evidence: This statement summarizes prior findings from the cited literature.

claim: The complexity of cell membranes obscured the simple conclusion that both PIP2 and Gβγ ligands are necessary to open the GIRK channel.
source: While past studies had reached the conclusion that both ligands are important—that one ligand enhances the affinity of the other (Huang et al., 1998; Yamada et al., 1998; Logothetis and Zhang, 1999)—the complexity of cell membranes obscured the simple conclusion so obvious here that both ligands are necessary to open the channel.
evidence: This is an interpretation comparing the clarity of the bilayer results to prior cell-based studies.

claim: The lipid anchor on Gβγ is essential for GIRK2 activation.
source: This experiment shows that the lipid anchor is essential.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the experimental observation in Figure 2F showing that non-lipidated Gβγ fails to robustly activate GIRK2.

claim: The lipid anchor is required to achieve sufficiently high enough concentrations of Gβγ on the membrane surface to activate GIRK2.
source: The likely explanation is, by mediating membrane partitioning, the lipid anchor is required to achieve sufficiently high enough concentrations of Gβγ on the membrane surface to activate GIRK2.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the experimental observation regarding the lipid anchor.

claim: Cellular electrophysiologists have referred to G protein activation of GIRK channels as 'membrane delimited'.
source: Cellular electrophysiologists have referred to G protein activation of GIRK channels as 'membrane delimited' (Soejima and Noma, 1984; Breitwieser and Szabo, 1985; Pfaffinger et al., 1985; Logothetis et al., 1987; Reuveny et al., 1994; Wickman et al., 1994), meaning Gβγ stays stuck to the membrane when it is released from a GPCR and diffuses to its target.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior electrophysiology literature.

claim: 'Membrane delimited' means Gβγ stays stuck to the membrane when it is released from a GPCR and diffuses to its target.
source: Cellular electrophysiologists have referred to G protein activation of GIRK channels as 'membrane delimited' (Soejima and Noma, 1984; Breitwieser and Szabo, 1985; Pfaffinger et al., 1985; Logothetis et al., 1987; Reuveny et al., 1994; Wickman et al., 1994), meaning Gβγ stays stuck to the membrane when it is released from a GPCR and diffuses to its target.
evidence: This is a definition of the term 'membrane delimited' as used in the field.

claim: The property of membrane targeting mediated by a lipid anchor is replicated in the bilayer assay.
source: Here, this property of membrane targeting mediated by a lipid anchor is nicely replicated in the bilayer assay.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental observations in Figure 2F.

claim: The importance of the lipid anchor is consistent with the orientation of Gβγ in the crystal structure, which shows the geranylgeranylated C-terminus of Gγ pointed toward the membrane.
source: The importance of the lipid anchor is also consistent with the orientation of Gβγ in the crystal structure, which shows the geranylgeranylated C-terminus of Gγ pointed toward the membrane (Figure 1A; Whorton and MacKinnon, 2013).
evidence: This statement connects the experimental observation to the structural data from a cited study.

claim: In the planar bilayer system channels and Gβγ subunits insert randomly and thus are oriented in both directions.
source: In contrast to the membranes of cells, in which channels are inserted with one orientation, in the planar bilayer system channels and Gβγ subunits insert randomly and thus are oriented in both directions.
evidence: This is a description of a property of the bilayer reconstitution system.

claim: Short chain C8-PIP2 activates only one orientation of GIRK2 channels—corresponding to those channels with their physiologically intracellular surface pointed toward the chamber to which PIP2 was added.
source: The experiments in Figure 3 show, despite the dual orientation of proteins in the bilayer membrane, that short chain C8-PIP2 activates only one orientation of GIRK2 channels—corresponding to those channels with their physiologically intracellular surface pointed toward the chamber to which PIP2 was added.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the experimental observations in Figure 3.

claim: TPNQ inhibits GIRK channels by binding to a specific receptor site on the extracellular surface of the channel.
source: TPNQ inhibits GIRK channels by binding to a specific receptor site on the extracellular surface of the channel.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge of TPNQ mechanism of action.

claim: When Gαi1 containing the non-hydrolyzable GTP analog GTPγS is applied to membranes containing GIRK channels there is no activation.
source: When Gαi1 containing the non-hydrolyzable GTP analog GTPγS is applied to membranes containing GIRK channels there is no activation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: GIRK2 channels are activated by Gβγ but not by Gαi1(GTPγS).
source: From this experiment it is clear that GIRK2 channels are activated by Gβγ but not by Gαi1(GTPγS), as summarized pictorially (Figure 4B).
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the experimental observations in Figure 4.

claim: GIRK2 channels are unresponsive to Gαi1(GTPγS) even after they have been activated by PIP2 and Gβγ.
source: Thus, GIRK2 channels are unresponsive to Gαi1(GTPγS) even after they have been activated by PIP2 and Gβγ.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the experimental observations in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Fusion of vesicles containing Gαi1(GDP) caused rapid disappearance of activated GIRK2 currents.
source: In contrast, fusion of vesicles containing Gαi1(GDP) caused rapid disappearance of activated GIRK2 currents (Figure 5C).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: At micromolar concentrations, soluble Gαi1(GDP) closed GIRK2 channels.
source: At micromolar concentrations, soluble Gαi1(GDP) closed GIRK2 channels, whereas soluble Gαi1(GTPγS) had only a small effect most likely due to small amounts of Gαi1(GDP) present in the Gαi1(GTPγS) preparation (Figure 5D).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Soluble Gαi1(GTPγS) had only a small effect on GIRK2 channels most likely due to small amounts of Gαi1(GDP) present in the Gαi1(GTPγS) preparation.
source: At micromolar concentrations, soluble Gαi1(GDP) closed GIRK2 channels, whereas soluble Gαi1(GTPγS) had only a small effect most likely due to small amounts of Gαi1(GDP) present in the Gαi1(GTPγS) preparation (Figure 5D).
evidence: This interpretation is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5D.

claim: Gαi1(GDP) in solution binds to membrane anchored Gβγ, rendering it unavailable to activate GIRK2.
source: Apparently Gαi1(GDP) in solution binds to membrane anchored Gβγ, rendering it unavailable to activate GIRK2, as depicted (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the experimental observations.

claim: The ability of soluble Gαi1(GDP) to close GIRK2 channels contrasts with the inability of soluble (lipid anchor-removed) Gβγ to open GIRK2 channels.
source: It is interesting to contrast the ability of soluble Gαi1(GDP) to close GIRK2 channels (Figure 5D) with the inability of soluble (lipid anchor-removed) Gβγ to open GIRK2 channels (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a comparison of two experimental observations from the study.

claim: The observation that soluble Gαi1(GDP) closes GIRK2 while soluble Gβγ does not open it suggests differences in the relative affinities of Gβγ for GIRK2 vs Gαi1(GDP).
source: This observation suggests differences in the relative affinities of Gβγ for GIRK2 vs Gαi1(GDP) (The equilibrium dissociation constant for Gαi1(GDP) binding to Gβγ is ∼3 nM in Lubrol and ∼10 nM in lipids [Sarvazyan et al., 1998]).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observations, supported by a citation to prior affinity measurements.

claim: The equilibrium dissociation constant for Gαi1(GDP) binding to Gβγ is ∼3 nM in Lubrol and ∼10 nM in lipids.
source: The equilibrium dissociation constant for Gαi1(GDP) binding to Gβγ is ∼3 nM in Lubrol and ∼10 nM in lipids [Sarvazyan et al., 1998]
evidence: This is a quantitative value cited from prior literature.

claim: Differential affinities of Gβγ for GIRK2 vs Gαi1(GDP) are likely important for G protein regulation of channel activity.
source: These differential affinities are likely important for G protein regulation of channel activity.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the affinity differences.

claim: The importance of the signaling lipid PIP2 to GIRK channel gating has been well documented through studies in cells.
source: The importance of the signaling lipid PIP2 to GIRK channel gating has been well documented through studies in cells (Huang et al., 1998; Sui et al., 1998; Rohacs et al., 2002; Gamper and Rohacs, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Previous studies augmented PIP2 levels in cell membranes through the addition of PIP2 to undetermined baseline levels or reduced PIP2 levels through the use of PIP2-sequestering antibodies.
source: Previous studies augmented PIP2 levels in cell membranes through the addition of PIP2 to undetermined baseline levels or reduced PIP2 levels through the use of PIP2-sequestering antibodies (Huang et al., 1998; Logothetis and Zhang, 1999; Rohacs et al., 2002; Inanobe et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement summarizes the approaches used in prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: Previous approaches yielded qualitative data on the relationship between GIRK channel activity and PIP2 concentration.
source: These approaches yielded qualitative data on the relationship between GIRK channel activity and PIP2 concentration.
evidence: This is a characterization of the limitations of prior studies.

claim: During perfusion of C8-PIP2 GIRK2 channels opened and during perfusion of buffer they closed as soluble C8-PIP2 diffused away from the membrane.
source: Soluble C8-PIP2 was then perfused with a microperfusion pipette aimed directly at the membrane to activate channels: during perfusion of C8-PIP2 channels opened and during perfusion of buffer they closed as soluble C8-PIP2 diffused away from the membrane (Figure 6A).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The activation curve of GIRK2 by C8-PIP2 follows a sigmoid shaped concentration dependence, consistent with activation by multiple PIP2 molecules.
source: The activation curve follows a sigmoid shaped concentration dependence, consistent with activation by multiple PIP2 molecules.
evidence: This is a description of the shape of the dose-response curve shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The atomic structure shows four PIP2 binding sites per GIRK2 channel.
source: The atomic structure shows four binding sites per channel (Figure 1A).
evidence: This statement refers to structural data from a cited study and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The shape of the PIP2 titration curve is consistent with multiple binding events being required for GIRK2 channel activation.
source: The most important point is that the shape of the titration curve is consistent with multiple binding events being required for channel activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of the dose-response data in Figure 6B.

claim: Hill fit of C8-PIP2 activation data gives an apparent dissociation constant of ∼15 μM and a Hill coefficient of ∼3.1.
source: Hill fit (solid line) gives an apparent dissociation constant of ∼15 μM and a Hill coefficient of ∼3.1.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from fitting the data in Figure 6B.

claim: Hill fit of brain PIP2 activation data resulted in an apparent dissociation constant of ∼0.8% mole fraction brain PIP2 and a Hill coefficient of ∼2.4.
source: Regression to Hill equation (solid line) resulted in an apparent dissociation constant of ∼0.8% mole fraction brain PIP2 and a Hill coefficient of ∼2.4.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from fitting the data in Figure 6D.

claim: The steepest portion of the PIP2 mole fraction dependence graph (corresponding to a few tenths to one percent PIP2) is in agreement with the known concentration range of PIP2 in the inner leaflet of cell membranes.
source: Moreover, the steepest portion of the graph (corresponding to a few tenths to one percent PIP2) is in agreement the known concentration range of PIP2 in the inner leaflet of cell membranes (Heck et al., 2007; van Meer et al., 2008; Balla, 2013).
evidence: This statement compares the experimental result to known values from cited literature.

claim: The PIP2 mole fraction dependence suggests that naturally occurring variations of PIP2 in cell membranes should influence GIRK2 activity level.
source: This mole fraction dependence suggests that naturally occurring variations of PIP2 in cell membranes should influence GIRK2 activity level.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of the quantitative PIP2 dependence.

claim: Intracellular Na+ was shown previously to be an activator of GIRK2 channels.
source: Intracellular Na+ was shown previously to be an activator of GIRK2 channels (Petit-Jacques et al., 1999; Ho and Murrell-Lagnado, 1999a, 1999b; Inanobe et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: GIRK2 channels open in the absence of internal Na+, but opening increases as the Na+ concentration is increased.
source: By contrast, GIRK2 channels open in the absence of internal Na+, but opening increases as the Na+ concentration is increased.
evidence: This observation is stated based on the data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The presence of internal Na+ steepens the dependence of GIRK2 channel opening on PIP2 concentration.
source: Viewed along the axis of PIP2 activation, the presence of internal Na+ steepens the dependence of channel opening on PIP2 concentration (Figure 7B).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Na+ is not essential but augments GIRK2 channel opening.
source: Thus, Na+ is not essential but augments channel opening.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the experimental observations in Figure 7.

claim: The effect of Na+ on GIRK2 depends on the degree of activation by PIP2.
source: The effect of Na+ depends on the degree of activation by PIP2.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the experimental observations in Figure 7.

claim: In the presence of ample PIP2, GIRK2 channel activity increases as a function of Na+ concentration most steeply in the range 0–10 mM.
source: In the presence of ample PIP2, channel activity increases as a function of Na+ concentration most steeply in the range 0–10 mM.
evidence: This observation is stated based on the data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The Na+ dependence of GIRK2 seems well matched to the concentration range over which cytoplasmic Na+ levels change in response to excessive electrical excitation.
source: This dependence seems well matched to the concentration range over which cytoplasmic Na+ levels change in response to excessive electrical excitation (Muller and Somjen, 2000; Somjen, 2002).
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the experimental result to physiological Na+ changes, supported by citations.

claim: Gα can interact physically with at least some GIRK channels.
source: One question addressed in this study, motivated by past work showing that Gα can interact physically with at least some GIRK channels (Yatani et al., 1988; Huang et al., 1995; Peleg et al., 2002; Ivanina et al., 2004; Berlin et al., 2011), concerns the role of Gα vs Gβγ in GIRK channel activation.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Gαi1(GTP) does not activate GIRK2.
source: Gαi1(GTP) does not activate GIRK2 and moreover does not appear to influence the activation of GIRK2 by Gβγ.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the experimental observations in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Gαi1(GTP) does not appear to influence the activation of GIRK2 by Gβγ.
source: Gαi1(GTP) does not activate GIRK2 and moreover does not appear to influence the activation of GIRK2 by Gβγ.
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the experimental observations in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Physical interactions between Gαi1(GTP) and GIRK2, if they indeed exist, are without direct functional consequence.
source: These findings suggest, at least for the case of the activated form of Gαi1 (Gαi1(GTP)) and GIRK2, that physical interactions between these proteins, if they indeed exist, are without direct functional consequence.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings regarding Gαi1(GTP).

claim: Gαi1 inhibits the GIRK2 channel activity only when it is in its GDP bound form, consistent with the canonical view that GIRK is activated by Gβγ and that GDP-bound Gαi1 sequesters Gβγ.
source: Gαi1 inhibits the GIRK2 channel activity only when it is in its GDP bound form, consistent with the canonical view that GIRK is activated by Gβγ and that GDP-bound Gαi1 sequesters Gβγ (Gilman, 1987; Wickman et al., 1994; Peleg et al., 2002).
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the experimental observations and is consistent with cited prior knowledge.

claim: The action of Gαi1(GDP) on GIRK2 in bilayer experiments is so rapid as to suggest that it might bind to the channel and cause Gβγ to dissociate.
source: In the bilayer experiments the action of Gαi1(GDP) is so rapid (Figure 5C) as to suggest that it might bind to the channel and cause Gβγ to dissociate.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the rapid kinetics observed in Figure 5C.

claim: A displacement mechanism need not be invoked to account for the rapid inhibitory effect of Gαi1(GDP) on GIRK2.
source: We think, however, that such a displacement mechanism need not be invoked to account for the rapid inhibitory effect of Gαi1(GDP).
evidence: This is a statement of the authors' interpretation of the mechanism.

claim: Gβγ fails to activate GIRK2 without a lipid anchor because, without membrane partitioning, its local concentration near the channel is never high enough to achieve sufficient occupancy to open the channel.
source: Presumably Gβγ fails under this circumstance because, without membrane partitioning, its local concentration near the channel is never high enough to achieve sufficient occupancy to open the channel.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the experimental observation regarding non-lipidated Gβγ.

claim: Gβγ apparently binds to the GIRK2 channel with low affinity, compatible with a rapid dissociation rate.
source: Thus, Gβγ apparently binds to the channel with low affinity, compatible with a rapid dissociation rate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations regarding lipid anchor requirement and the ability of Gαi1(GDP) to sequester Gβγ.

claim: Gβγ appears to bind Gαi1(GDP) with high affinity, as this would account for sequestration of Gβγ even when no lipid is present on Gαi1(GDP).
source: Comparatively, Gβγ appears to bind Gαi1(GDP) with high affinity, as this would account for sequestration of Gβγ even when no lipid is present on Gαi1(GDP) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observation in Figure 5D.

claim: It seems likely that Gαi1(GDP) turns off GIRK by simply binding to the free (channel unbound) form of Gβγ and shifting the equilibrium away from channel occupancy by Gβγ.
source: Therefore, it seems likely that Gαi1(GDP) turns off GIRK by simply binding to the free (channel unbound) form of Gβγ and shifting the equilibrium away from channel occupancy by Gβγ.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the experimental observations and inferred affinity differences.

claim: During biochemical purification a complex between GIRK2 and Gβγ has never been detected on gel filtration even when both proteins are at concentrations in the 100 µM range.
source: During biochemical purification we have never detected a complex between these two proteins on gel filtration even when both proteins are at concentrations in the 100 µM range (Whorton and MacKinnon, 2013).
evidence: This is a statement of an experimental observation from the authors' prior work.

claim: Using solution NMR spectroscopy, Shimada et al. estimated the affinity between Gβγ and the GIRK1 cytoplasmic domain to be about 250 μM.
source: Using solution NMR spectroscopy, Shimada et al. estimated the affinity between Gβγ and the GIRK1 cytoplasmic domain (which accounts for the full protein–protein interaction surface) to be about 250 μM (Yokogawa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a quantitative value cited from prior literature.

claim: If we conservatively assume an association rate of 105 M−1s−1 for Gβγ binding to GIRK2, then the dwell time for a single Gβγ on the channel is calculated to be about 100 ms.
source: Using this value, if we conservatively assume an association rate of 105 M−1s−1 (well below the expected diffusion limit in solution) then the dwell time for a single Gβγ on the channel is calculated to be about 100 ms, a duration much shorter than the wash out time in our experiments.
evidence: This is a calculation based on assumed kinetic parameters and cited affinity values.

claim: A low affinity interaction between Gβγ and GIRK2 matches the relatively small surface area (∼700 Å2) of interaction between Gβγ and its binding site on GIRK2 in the crystal structure.
source: Finally, a low affinity interaction matches the relatively small surface area (∼700 Å2) of interaction between Gβγ and its binding site on GIRK2 in the crystal structure (Whorton and MacKinnon, 2013).
evidence: This statement connects the inferred low affinity to structural data from a cited study.

claim: All observations are consistent with the idea that Gβγ is in rapid exchange with its binding site on the GIRK channel.
source: Therefore, all observations are consistent with the idea that Gβγ is in rapid exchange with its binding site on the GIRK channel.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence presented.

claim: GPCR activation generates Gβγ and Gα(GTP), then Gβγ activates GIRK, but once GTP is hydrolyzed the resultant Gα(GDP) removes Gβγ from the channel by equilibrium-mass action.
source: GPCR activation generates Gβγ and Gα(GTP), then Gβγ activates GIRK, but once GTP is hydrolyzed the resultant Gα(GDP) removes Gβγ from the channel by equilibrium-mass action.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: It seems unlikely that a single GPCR located near a GIRK channel would be able to generate a high enough local concentration of subunits to activate it, especially if multiple bound Gβγ subunits are required.
source: It seems unlikely that a single GPCR located near a GIRK channel would be able to generate a high enough local concentration of subunits to activate it, especially if multiple bound Gβγ subunits are required, which we suspect is the case on the basis of the crystal structure (Whorton and MacKinnon, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the requirements for GIRK activation in cells.

claim: Multiple bound Gβγ subunits are required for GIRK2 activation, which is suspected on the basis of the crystal structure.
source: It seems unlikely that a single GPCR located near a GIRK channel would be able to generate a high enough local concentration of subunits to activate it, especially if multiple bound Gβγ subunits are required, which we suspect is the case on the basis of the crystal structure (Whorton and MacKinnon, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural data from a cited study.

claim: GIRK channels and GPCRs might be co-localized in relatively large patches on the membrane.
source: One way to explain this dilemma is to imagine that GIRK channels and GPCRs might be co-localized in relatively large patches on the membrane.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed to explain how GIRK activation could occur in cells.

claim: A point source in an infinite 2-dimensional space has no steady state solution.
source: Such an organization would exploit a fundamental property of 2-dimensional diffusion: a point source in an infinite space has no steady state solution.
evidence: This is a statement of a mathematical property of 2D diffusion.

claim: The transition between local and bulk Gβγ concentration will grow radially with activation time in a patch of multiple GPCRs.
source: In other words, the transition between local and bulk Gβγ concentration will grow radially with activation time.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of 2D diffusion.

claim: In a patch of multiple GPCRs (and channels) a sufficiently high concentration of Gβγ on the membrane could be reached.
source: Thus, in a patch of multiple GPCRs (and channels) a sufficiently high concentration of Gβγ on the membrane could be reached.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the diffusion argument.

claim: The possibility of co-localization of GPCRs and GIRK channels raises an interesting challenge to the replication of cell-like signaling in the bilayer.
source: The possibility of co-localization of GPCRs and GIRK channels raises an interesting challenge to the replication of cell-like signaling in the bilayer.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the co-localization hypothesis for the bilayer system.

claim: Additional cellular elements (e.g., cytoskeleton) might be required to perfectly replicate the signaling behavior observed in cells.
source: It could be that additional cellular elements (e.g., cytoskeleton) are required to perfectly replicate the signaling behavior observed in cells.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential limitations of the bilayer system.

claim: When PIP2 alone is bound to GIRK2 the channel's inner gate remains closed (it exhibits the same closed conformation as when PIP2 is not bound).
source: This conclusion is beautifully compatible with structural studies of GIRK2, which show that when PIP2 alone is bound the channel's inner gate remains closed (it exhibits the same closed conformation as when PIP2 is not bound) (Whorton and MacKinnon, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to a prior structural study.

claim: When both Gβγ and PIP2 are bound to GIRK2 the cytoplasmic domain rotates with respect to the transmembrane domain and causes the inner helix gate to begin opening.
source: But when both Gβγ and PIP2 are bound the cytoplasmic domain rotates with respect to the transmembrane domain and causes the inner helix gate to begin opening (Whorton and MacKinnon, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to a prior structural study.

claim: PIP2 binds near the interface between the cytoplasmic domain and the transmembrane domain of GIRK2.
source: PIP2 binds near the interface between the cytoplasmic domain and the transmembrane domain.
evidence: This is a statement based on structural data from cited studies.

claim: PIP2 strengthens allosteric communication between the cytoplasmic domain and the transmembrane domain of GIRK2.
source: We hypothesize that PIP2 strengthens allosteric communication between these two domains of the channel.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the mechanism of PIP2 action.

claim: Strengthening of interaction between domains by PIP2 would allow conformational changes in the cytoplasmic domain, induced by Gβγ binding, to open the gate in the transmembrane domain.
source: Such a strengthening of interaction would allow conformational changes in the cytoplasmic domain, induced by Gβγ binding, to open the gate in the transmembrane domain.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on the proposed hypothesis.

claim: Na+ increases GIRK2 channel opening in the presence of Gβγ and PIP2 and thus Na+ is best described as a modulator of the other ligands' effects.
source: Na+ increases channel opening in the presence of Gβγ and PIP2 and thus Na+ is best described as a modulator of the other ligands' effects (Figure 7C).
evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the experimental observations in Figure 7.

claim: Na+ does not simply scale the PIP2 dependence curve of GIRK2 activation.
source: Not only does Na+ increase the current level at any given concentration of PIP2 (and a fixed concentration of Gβγ), but the shape of the PIP2 dependence curve is affected by Na+. In other words, Na+ does not simply scale the PIP2 dependence curve.
evidence: This observation is stated based on the data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The binding affinity/effect of PIP2 on GIRK2 is coupled to the presence of Na+.
source: This is explicable if the binding affinity/effect of PIP2 is coupled to the presence of Na+ (Ho and Murrell-Lagnado, 1999a, 1999b).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observation, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In the crystal structure Na+ binds at a location in between Gβγ and PIP2 on GIRK2.
source: In the crystal structure Na+ binds at a location in between Gβγ and PIP2.
evidence: This is a statement based on structural data from cited studies.

claim: It is reasonable to think that conformational changes induced by the binding of one ligand (e.g., Na+) would have consequences for the binding/effect of another ligand (e.g., Gβγ or PIP2) on GIRK2.
source: It is therefore reasonable to think that conformational changes induced by the binding of one ligand, for example Na+, would have consequences for the binding/effect of another ligand, for example Gβγ or PIP2.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the structural location of Na+ binding.

claim: Although Na+ plays a modulatory rather than obligatory role in GIRK2 gating, its effect is substantial and occurs over the range in which cytoplasmic Na+ concentration is known to change when a cell is experiencing excessive electrical excitation.
source: Although Na+ plays a modulatory rather than obligatory role in gating, its effect is substantial and occurs over the range in which cytoplasmic Na+ concentration is known to change when a cell is experiencing excessive electrical excitation (Muller and Somjen, 2000).
evidence: This statement connects the experimental findings to physiological Na+ changes, supported by citation.

claim: The findings on Na+ modulation are in good agreement with the hypothesis that Na+ modulation renders GIRK2 a negative feedback safety element.
source: These findings are in good agreement with the hypothesis that Na+ modulation renders GIRK2 a negative feedback safety element (Ho and Murrell-Lagnado, 1999a).
evidence: This statement connects the experimental findings to a prior hypothesis, supported by citation.

claim: The dual requirement for both Gβγ and PIP2 may have important consequences for the control of cellular electrical excitability by different signaling pathways.
source: The dual requirement for both Gβγ and PIP2 may have important consequences for the control of cellular electrical excitability by different signaling pathways.
evidence: This is a statement about the functional implications of the dual ligand requirement.

claim: Gβγ is released upon stimulation of all GPCRs.
source: Consider that Gβγ is released upon stimulation of all GPCRs, but GIRK channels only open specifically in response to Gi/o coupled GPCRs (Gi/o refers to G protein trimers containing i/o class Gα subunits) (Breitwieser and Szabo, 1985; Pfaffinger et al., 1985).
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge of GPCR signaling.

claim: GIRK channels only open specifically in response to Gi/o coupled GPCRs.
source: Consider that Gβγ is released upon stimulation of all GPCRs, but GIRK channels only open specifically in response to Gi/o coupled GPCRs (Gi/o refers to G protein trimers containing i/o class Gα subunits) (Breitwieser and Szabo, 1985; Pfaffinger et al., 1985).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Gq coupled GPCRs release Gβγ, but at the same time the Gαq subunit activates PLC, which depletes PIP2 through hydrolysis.
source: Gq coupled GPCRs release Gβγ, but at the same time the Gαq subunit activates PLC, which depletes PIP2 through hydrolysis (Cho et al., 2005; Keselman et al., 2007; Sohn et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In the absence of sufficient PIP2, Gβγ cannot activate GIRK.
source: In the absence of sufficient PIP2, Gβγ cannot activate GIRK.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings of the study.

claim: Recent experiments have shown in both atrial pacemaker cells and certain neurons that Gq coupled GPCR stimulation inhibits GIRK activation by Gi/o coupled GPCR stimulation.
source: Indeed, recent experiments have shown in both atrial pacemaker cells (Cho et al., 2005) and certain neurons (Sohn et al., 2007; Yamamoto et al., 2014) that Gq coupled GPCR stimulation inhibits GIRK activation by Gi/o coupled GPCR stimulation.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: It is reasonable to think that absence of PIP2 accounts at least in part for the inability of Gq coupled GPCRs to activate GIRK.
source: It is thus reasonable to think that absence of PIP2 accounts at least in part for the inability of Gq coupled GPCRs to activate GIRK.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the experimental findings to the GPCR selectivity phenomenon.

claim: Gi/o coupled GPCRs generate Gβγ without degrading PIP2 so both necessary ligands are available to activate GIRK.
source: Gi/o coupled GPCRs on the other hand generate Gβγ without degrading PIP2 so both necessary ligands are available to activate GIRK.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on known properties of Gi/o signaling and the experimental findings.

claim: GPCR selectivity for GIRK activation results because GIRK is an AND gate with respect to Gβγ and PIP2 activation.
source: This kind of GPCR selectivity results because GIRK is an AND gate with respect to Gβγ and PIP2 activation.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation of GPCR selectivity based on the experimental findings.

claim: AND gating of GPCR targets by multiple ligands provides a mechanism for selectivity in G protein signaling.
source: In addition to the more widespread (but not yet proved) idea of GPCR/target protein co-localization (Fowler et al., 2007; Labouebe et al., 2007; Cui et al., 2010; Luscher and Slesinger, 2010), AND gating of GPCR targets by multiple ligands provides a mechanism for selectivity in G protein signaling.
evidence: This is a general conclusion about signaling selectivity mechanisms, supported by the experimental findings and citations.

claim: Mouse GIRK2 (amino acid residues 52–380) was expressed in Pichia pastoris cells.
source: Mouse GIRK2 (amino acid residues 52–380) was expressed in Pichia pastoris cells, extracted with decyl-β-D-maltopyranoside (DM) and purified as previously described (Whorton and MacKinnon, 2011).
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental methods used.

claim: PIP2 activated GIRK2 currents were ∼2.5-fold higher (at 28 μM C8-PIP2) in the presence of 32 mM Na+ compared to absence of Na+.
source: PIP2 activated GIRK2 currents were ∼2.5-fold higher (at 28 μM) in the presence of 32 mM Na+.
evidence: This quantitative observation is stated in the Figure 7B legend.

claim: Hill fitting of PIP2 activation data in the presence of 32 mM Na+ resulted in apparent dissociation constant of ∼12 μM and Hill coefficient of ∼1.5.
source: Hill fitting resulted in apparent dissociation constants of ∼15 μM and ∼12 μM and Hill coefficients of ∼3.1 and ∼1.5 in the absence and presence of Na+, respectively.
evidence: This quantitative result is stated in the Figure 7B legend.

claim: The Na+ titration data were fit to a simple 1:1 dose response model with an apparent dissociation constant of ∼9 mM.
source: The titration data were fit to a simple 1:1 dose response model with an apparent dissociation constant of ∼9 mM.
evidence: This quantitative result is stated in the Figure 7C legend.
